spots.name: Hawk Hill (Conzelman Road)
spots.blurb: The single most photographed climb in the Bay Area — the Marin Headlands road up from the Golden Gate Bridge's north end to the Hawk Hill summit, with the bridge and city framed behind. A fixture of San Francisco Grand Prix-era racing and the standard Saturday effort for every SF club.
spots.notes: West of the summit Conzelman is one-way downhill — 17 of its 20 ways carry oneway=yes — so the descent toward Point Bonita has no oncoming traffic. Popular with tourists and often busy.

spots.name: Old La Honda Road
spots.blurb: The Bay Area's benchmark climb and de facto fitness test: the 5.6 km east side from Portola Road to Skyline is the most-ridden timed segment on the Peninsula, with a sub-15-minute time the long-standing marker of a serious amateur.
spots.notes: Narrow, no centerline, and damp under redwoods much of the year — the descent is technical rather than fast. The bbox covers both sides of Skyline.

spots.name: Mount Diablo — South Gate Road
spots.blurb: The lower half of the Bay Area's premier mountain climb and the route of the Mt. Diablo Challenge, run every October since 1982 — the 17.7 km race from Athenian School to the summit where breaking one hour earns you the 'under an hour' shirt.
spots.notes: State park road: entrance fee for cars, and the gates close at sunset.

spots.name: Mount Diablo — Summit Road
spots.blurb: The upper mountain — from Junction Ranger Station to the 1,173 m summit, including the notorious final pitch to the observation tower that decides the Mt. Diablo Challenge every year.
spots.notes: Ice and seasonal closures near the top.

spots.name: Marin Avenue (Berkeley)
spots.blurb: The steepest sustained paved street climb in the Bay Area — the arrow-straight wall from Arlington Avenue to Grizzly Peak Boulevard, pitching to roughly 25%, and a rite of passage for East Bay cyclists.
spots.notes: Real traffic, and cross streets with stop signs the whole way down. Steep enough that the descent is genuinely brake-limited rather than fast.

spots.name: Twin Peaks Boulevard
spots.blurb: San Francisco's signature summit road and one of the city's classic skate bombs — the switchbacked drop from the 280 m overlook into the Castro, with the whole city laid out ahead.
spots.notes: The north loop is now the car-free Twin Peaks Promenade; OSM tags it as construction/pedestrian, so the pathfinder won't route onto it and the road may come back fragmented. Fog and wind are constant.

spots.name: Dolores Street
spots.blurb: The most famous street skate bomb in San Francisco — the palm-lined drop from Dolores Heights through the Mission, immortalized by the annual unsanctioned hill bombs that draw hundreds of skaters.
spots.notes: Legally fraught: SFPD has repeatedly cracked down on the Dolores bombs, with mass citations and arrests in 2023. A divided boulevard with real traffic, stop signs and Muni — each carriageway is a separate one-way OSM way.

spots.name: Filbert Street (Russian Hill)
spots.blurb: Tied with 22nd Street as the steepest street in San Francisco at a surveyed 31.5% — the Hyde-to-Leavenworth block on Russian Hill, steep enough that the city paved it in concrete with traction ridges and the sidewalks are stairs.
spots.notes: One extreme block, not a sustained run. Concrete with transverse traction ridges — rough and grabby on urethane. Expect Hillbomb to under-read the grade here: 10 m elevation data smooths a 31.5% pitch to about 14%.

spots.name: Bradford Street (Bernal Heights)
spots.blurb: Widely cited as the steepest street in San Francisco — and arguably in the US — at a claimed 41% on the short dead-end pitch above Tompkins Avenue, on the north face of Bernal Heights.
spots.notes: The 41% is a claim, not a survey, and applies only to a short dead-end stub rather than the street as a whole. It doesn't connect through: a stunt pitch, not a descent with a run-out.

spots.name: Page Mill Road (upper)
spots.blurb: One of the Peninsula's great sustained climbs, rising from Palo Alto to Skyline Boulevard past Foothills Park — a Silicon Valley classic and the standard long effort paired with Old La Honda.
spots.notes: The lower half of Page Mill is an expressway; this is the upper road only.

spots.name: Sierra Road
spots.blurb: The decisive climb of the Amgen Tour of California — the brutally exposed wall above East San Jose that shattered the peloton on multiple editions and remains the Bay Area's hardest big climb.
spots.notes: No shade and no water, but a fast, open descent.

spots.name: Mount Tamalpais — Ridgecrest Boulevard
spots.blurb: The ridge road along Mt. Tamalpais to the East Peak — the mountain where mountain biking was invented, the Repack downhill running nearby — and the most scenic paved descent in Marin.
spots.notes: Ridgecrest is the ridge road: rolling, with a low average grade. The real elevation is gained below it on Panoramic Highway. Gated in fire weather.

spots.name: Baxter Street (Echo Park)
spots.blurb: One of the steepest streets in the United States at about 32%, famous well beyond cycling: the blind crest became a viral Waze-routing disaster, with cars bottoming out and crashing often enough that LA restricted it in 2019.
spots.notes: The crest is genuinely blind — drivers cannot see over it, which is exactly what makes bombing it dangerous. Concrete on the steep blocks.

spots.name: Eldred Street (Highland Park)
spots.blurb: Frequently ranked the steepest street in Los Angeles at about 33% — so steep it dead-ends in a staircase, garbage trucks refuse to drive it, and the city serves it with a special small vehicle.
spots.notes: A dead end that finishes in stairs. Very short, narrow, and no run-out.

spots.name: Fargo Street (Echo Park)
spots.blurb: Home of the Fargo Street Hill Climb, run by the Los Angeles Wheelmen every year since 1974 — the oldest 'can you even ride up it' event in American cycling, on a roughly 32% pitch where most entrants fail.
spots.notes: Concrete, and on the same Echo Park hill as Baxter Street.

spots.name: Glendora Mountain Road
spots.blurb: 'GMR' — the most-ridden mountain road in Southern California and the training ground for generations of LA racers: 24 km of near-constant gradient above Glendora, immaculate surface, legendary descent.
spots.notes: Subject to fire and storm closures that have lasted years at a time. Heavy motorcycle traffic on weekends. The largest bbox in the collection — expect a slow first build.

spots.name: Latigo Canyon Road
spots.blurb: The best-known climb in the Santa Monica Mountains — 16 km of switchbacks from Pacific Coast Highway to the ridge, a staple of Malibu gran fondos and the descent that defines Malibu road riding.
spots.notes: The drop back to PCH is fast and open, with long sightlines.

spots.name: Tuna Canyon Road
spots.blurb: Roughly 70 turns in four miles dropping to the Pacific — and most of it is legally one-way downhill, a legacy of an old mudslide, so you get the whole road with no oncoming traffic. One of the most sought-after descents in California for cyclists and longboarders alike.
spots.notes: The one-way-downhill status is the entire appeal, but OSM's tagging doesn't reflect it: only 1 of 7 ways carries oneway=yes and one is explicitly oneway=no, so the pathfinder may route it in both directions. Narrow, blind turns, no guardrail.

spots.name: Piuma Road
spots.blurb: A Santa Monica Mountains classic climbed from Malibu Canyon, and one of the most consistently used race-simulation climbs for LA-area cyclists.
spots.notes: Pairs with Stunt Road on the standard Malibu loop.

spots.name: Stunt Road
spots.blurb: One of the definitive Santa Monica Mountains climbs, running from Mulholland Highway to Saddle Peak — a fixture of Malibu loops and a well-known motorcycle and cycling road.
spots.notes: Good surface, technical descent.

spots.name: Queen Anne Avenue North (the Counterbalance)
spots.blurb: 'The Counterbalance' — named for the underground 16-ton counterweights that hauled streetcars up this ~18% grade from 1900 to 1940. The tunnels are still under the street. Seattle's most storied hill.
spots.notes: A busy arterial with real traffic and signals at Mercer and Roy.

spots.name: Lookout Mountain Road
spots.blurb: Colorado's most-ridden climb — the switchbacks out of Golden past Buffalo Bill's grave, used by the Coors Classic and the USA Pro Challenge, and the daily proving ground for the Front Range.
spots.notes: Tagged bicycle=designated on several ways, with wide shoulders. The descent into Golden is fast, open and well-sighted.

spots.name: Flagstaff Road (Flagstaff Mountain)
spots.blurb: Boulder's iconic climb, rising straight out of Chautauqua Park — a regular USA Pro Challenge summit finish and probably the most famous training climb in American cycling, ridden by decades of Boulder-based pros.
spots.notes: Steep, tight switchbacks low down make for a technical descent.

spots.name: Maryhill Loops Road
spots.blurb: The most famous downhill skateboarding road in America. Built in 1911 as Washington's first asphalt road, it's now owned by the Maryhill Museum, closed to cars most of the year, and rented to longboard clubs — 2.1 miles and 21 bends of pristine, traffic-free pavement.
spots.notes: A private road owned by the Maryhill Museum. Skating it requires a paid, waivered event — you cannot just show up and bomb it.
